splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) in interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity should take priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions that expand criminal liability or sentencing enhancements. This matters because it determines whether ambiguity in criminal sentencing guidelines is resolved in favor of the defendant or the government's preferred interpretation.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference in criminal contexts, meaning ambiguity should be resolved in favor of the defendant rather than deferring to the government's interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity, allowing the government's anti-defendant interpretation to control when Guidelines commentary or regulations are ambiguous.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether USSG § 4B1.2(b)'s definition of 'controlled substance offense' unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, such that Application Note 1 (which includes them) exceeds the Sentencing Commission's interpretive authority under Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is entitled to deference or impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects thousands of federal drug defendants whose sentences depend on whether prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career-offender predicates.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and receives deference
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text is ambiguous regarding inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt is a reasonable interpretation entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly adds to, rather than interprets, the guideline, meaning it is not entitled to deference.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Lopez (circuit split noted)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Courts are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history disqualifiers in § 3553(f)(1) to be ineligible for safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This affects whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums for many drug offenders, leading to dramatically different sentences depending on the circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are satisfied.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that meeting any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, interpreting 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state controls a substance not listed on federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally scheduled or whether any state-law controlled substance conviction qualifies. This affects the career-offender and other enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances not on federal schedules.

positions.label: State-scheduled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that USSG § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state-law offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally controlled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Only federally scheduled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under federal law, applying a categorical approach that requires federal-state overlap.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. De Jesus Ventura

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts may consider non-retroactive statutory sentencing changes as a factor supporting compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes can never be extraordinary and compelling reasons, while others permit them to be considered alone or in combination with other factors. This affects thousands of prisoners serving stacked § 924(c) sentences that would be much shorter under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered, alone or combined with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting a sentence reduction, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement at USSG § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) or may use civil rights actions (Bivens) to challenge conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody, such as First Step Act time-credit determinations.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to prison conditions or BOP administrative decisions affecting release dates must be brought as habeas petitions or may proceed as civil rights claims. This affects prisoners' procedural rights, including exhaustion requirements and available remedies.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-of-confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP decisions affecting release timing, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights actions to challenge conditions or terms of confinement even when habeas may also be available, particularly where the challenge does not solely seek release.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Nettles v. Grounds (noted in Fortner split discussion)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees filed in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though filed in a criminal case, is a civil matter subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline or a criminal matter subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises from and is filed in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Manzo (noted in Onamuti as minority view)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in asset equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value occurring between the Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This has major implications for homeowners who convert bankruptcies during rising housing markets.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, and § 348(f)(1)(A) does not carve out an exception for equity increases.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to debtors who convert in good faith, consistent with the statute's structure, policies, and legislative history protecting good-faith converters.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: In re Boggs (noted in Castleman dissent as contrary authority)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit, under its Lewis precedent, permits courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the 'extreme of a circuit split.' Other circuits hold that revocation sanctions must be premised on the breach of trust, not punishment for the underlying violation conduct. This affects hundreds of supervised release revocations annually.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying a supervised release violation, not just for breaching the court's trust.

positions.label: Revocation must be based on breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sanctions should be based on the defendant's breach of the court's trust, consistent with the sanctioning purposes of supervised release as distinct from the original sentence of imprisonment.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Dees (noted in Esteras dissent)

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: This split concerns the timing of when actuarial assumptions must be selected for calculating employer withdrawal liability under ERISA's multiemployer pension provisions. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select or update actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in by year-end.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Related ERISA withdrawal liability cases (noted in cert petition)

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises fundamental questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during absconding, allowing the court to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release runs continuously and is not tolled by absconding, as no statute authorizes judicial extension of the release term beyond what the judgment specifies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, and they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on how to evaluate whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome affects whether candidates can challenge rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before an election takes place.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury from election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter election outcomes, granting them standing to challenge such laws pre-election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that the speculative nature of pre-election competitive harm is insufficient to establish Article III injury-in-fact, and that candidates' claimed injuries are too generalized or conjectural.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Related election standing cases (noted in cert proceedings)

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether orders denying motions to seal documents containing private medical information are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying sealing of medical records are immediately appealable as collateral orders because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Other circuits may not extend the collateral order doctrine this broadly, creating potential divergence on what privacy interests justify interlocutory appeal.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical information qualify as collateral orders because maintaining medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders, even involving medical privacy, are not the type of orders that the collateral order doctrine was designed to cover, as they can be reviewed after final judgment.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Kravetz (noted in Abdelhady as recognizing medical privacy interest but not extending collateral order doctrine)

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to legal questions governing how business operators must treat customers and what remedies are available for discrimination or unfair treatment was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review, suggesting a circuit split on the applicable standards. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied standards for discrimination liability and damages in hospitality contexts that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or divergent from other circuits to warrant review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims and available remedies in the hospitality or business establishment context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
